title: Still Operational
paragraphs: The first sound Andrew Walker heard that morning was someone singing in the corridor.

It was a terrible song. Not because the singer lacked enthusiasm. There was far too much enthusiasm for six in the morning, and whoever had invented the tune hadn't bothered with the inconvenience of a melody.
Andrew opened one eye.
Across the little room, Nicolas Vallée lay faceup on his bunk with a pillow pressed over his head. One hand emerged long enough to give the ceiling an offended gesture.
“Tell him,” Nico said through the pillow.
“Tell him what?”
“That his kitchen is on the other side of the building.”
The singing continued, followed by a metallic crash and a very recognizable voice saying, “I'm all right.”
Andrew pulled his blanket higher. “I think he's figured that out.”
“He hasn't. He's singing again.”

The room had been an office before the war. There was still a painted rectangle on the wall where a noticeboard had hung, and the two beds had to be arranged foot-to-foot because there wasn't room to put them any other way. Someone had screwed a narrow shelf above Andrew's pillow. It held a torch, two paperback books, and a clock whose green numerals insisted that it was 06:14.
He was nineteen. He had been in charge of their outpost for almost four months. Neither fact had made mornings any easier.
From outside came three impatient knocks.
“Andrew?” Darius called. “Are you awake?”
“No,” Andrew said.
“Good. I need a second opinion.”
“On what?”
“Something I made.”
Nico removed the pillow. His dark curls stuck up on one side. “Tell him you're dead.”
“Then he'll make enough for seven.”
“That would be a kindness.”

Andrew sat up. His uniform trousers hung from the end of the bed; his boots stood underneath them, close enough to reach without stepping on the cold floor. The heater had gone off again in the night. The military could provide eight trained mech pilots and a building full of expensive equipment, but it apparently couldn't maintain a radiator.
He pulled on his socks and opened the door.

Darius Okafor filled most of the passage. He was wearing an apron over his base clothes and holding a spoon with a smear of something pale and thick on it. Behind him, the converted depot stretched away in a line of old offices. The windows were wet with rain. A yellow emergency lamp burned at the far end of the hall, illuminating a sign that read CONSERVE POWER in three languages.
Darius offered the spoon.
Andrew stared at it. “What is it?”
“Breakfast.”
“That's not an answer.”
“It's supposed to be porridge.”
“Supposed to be?”
“I'd like an unbiased assessment before I tell you what went into it.”
Andrew considered the spoon. Darius was tall enough that Andrew had to look up slightly, and his expression was so hopeful that refusing felt worse than whatever was in the bowl.
He tasted it.
For a moment he could identify oats. Then came cinnamon, something sour, and a flavor that he had no intention of guessing.
Darius watched his face.
“That's interesting,” Andrew said.
“Interesting good?”
“Interesting in a historical sense. People will talk about it.”
From behind Andrew, Nico called, “Ask him whether it can strip paint.”
Darius leaned around the doorframe. “I heard that.”
“You were meant to,” Nico said.
Darius took back the spoon, looking more thoughtful than insulted. “I used the powdered milk.”
“Did you check the label?” Andrew asked.
“Of course.”
“Both sides?”
Darius glanced down at his spoon.
Andrew knew that look. It was the same expression people wore when they remembered an exam question two minutes after handing in the paper.
“Breakfast at seven,” Darius said, and departed at speed.
Nico swung his legs off the bed. “He'll be fine. He still has forty minutes to invent a new one.”
“He had forty minutes,” Andrew said. “Now he has thirty-six.”
He shut the door before Nico could throw the pillow.

By the time Andrew reached the washroom, the building had begun waking around him. Pipes clicked in the walls. Someone had turned on the radio in the common room. Through the washroom's steamed-up window he could see the hangar beyond the courtyard, a long concrete structure with two wide doors and rainwater gathering in the cracks of the apron.
Eight XR-17s lived there, if lived was the word for machines that required more attention than the people operating them.

Their base had once been a municipal maintenance depot. Now concrete barriers divided the vehicle yard, cables ran along the outer walls, and a pair of watch posts looked east across empty fields. Beyond those fields lay the routes used by the Reclaimed, human-and-machine creatures that advanced with the coordination of a single mind. The creatures had driven the survivors of other countries into the last defended territory. Beyond the defenses, to the west, were the towns and crowded cities that humanity still held.
The rest of the world was gone to them. Germany was where the survivors had gathered, and the XR-17s were one of the reasons a refuge still existed at all.
Andrew brushed his teeth, rinsed the sink, and decided that those facts were easier to contemplate after breakfast.
When he entered the common room, Akari Sato was taking a photograph of an empty chair.
She stood with her camera raised, long black ponytail hanging over the shoulder of a faded sweatshirt. She moved sideways, frowned at the display, and tried again.
Andrew looked from her to the chair. “Did it do something worth remembering?”
“I'm testing the light.”
“On a chair?”
“It's a very patient subject.”
“Unlike the rest of us?”
Akari lowered the camera. “Exactly. Also, don't make plans for this afternoon.”
“I already have plans.”
“Cancel them.”
“My plans include ensuring the machines that keep us alive continue doing so.”
“Good. Then you'll already be at the hangar.”
Andrew stopped reaching for the coffee tin. “Akari.”
“Group picture,” she said. “Outside. In front of the mechs. Everybody.”
“We have pictures.”
“We have old pictures.”
“Photographs generally work that way.”
Akari gave him the smile she used when she had decided an argument was already over. “Four o'clock. If the rain stops.”
Andrew found the coffee tin empty.
“Do I get a vote?” he asked.
“You can vote on where to stand.”
He turned the tin upside down anyway. A few grains fell into his palm.
Akari watched him with genuine sympathy. “That's heartbreaking.”
“Are you going to photograph this too?”
“Only if you cry.”

The doorway opened again. Mara Venn entered carrying a waterproof map case under one arm. Her long chestnut hair was tied back, and her boots had brought half the courtyard with her. She looked at the empty coffee tin in Andrew's hand and set a small, still-sealed packet beside it.
“From the watch post,” Mara said. “They owed me.”
Andrew lifted it reverently. “I'm putting you in charge of morale.”
“No, thank you. That's your problem.”

Mara had been outside checking the eastern access road before most of the building stirred. She had made a note of the morning's rainfall on the route sheet and had her usual list of things to complain about, which meant she was in a good mood by Mara's standards.
“Tomorrow's patrol,” she said, tapping the map case. “We need to talk before Juno takes his machine out.”
“Something wrong with the route?”
“Something wrong with half the route.”
Akari pointed her camera at them.
“Not now,” Andrew and Mara said together.
Akari took the picture anyway.
The second breakfast was better.

Darius replaced the porridge with toasted bread, beans warmed in a pan, and a bowl of chopped apples that he had coaxed from a driver the previous week. The apples had a few soft spots, but everybody took some. In their part of the country, fresh fruit wasn't something you left behind because it looked imperfect.
Nico arrived carrying two plates and claimed the largest pieces of toast by moving them onto his own before setting anything down.
Darius caught him in the act.
“Those are for everyone,” Darius said.
“I'm part of everyone.”
“You're the part that hasn't helped.”
“I gave moral support during the porridge crisis.”
“You laughed.”
“With feeling.”
Andrew slid one of Nico's plates back toward the middle. “We appreciate your service.”
Nico made a face, but he let the plate go.

Mara spread her map across the table after the dishes had been cleared. Andrew moved his coffee away from the paper. Rain pressed softly against the high windows, and the radio on the shelf murmured through the morning bulletin. There were reports of another road closure farther east and the familiar request for civilians to conserve fuel. Nobody turned the volume up.
A thick blue pencil line crossed the map, following the patrol route from their depot to a relay station near the outer defensive works.

“The approach here has gone under,” Mara said. Her finger rested on the eastern crossing. “The water's already against the road markers. If the river keeps rising, we won't get a recovery vehicle through.”
“Can an XR-17 cross it?” Andrew asked.
“Probably. But if one of us has to tow another one home, we'd be stuck.”

Andrew pictured the route from memory. An open stretch of road, a narrow bridge, and a bend that concealed the next field until a pilot was almost on top of it. He had liked the direct approach because it kept the unit in sight of the observation post for most of the journey.
“Service road?” he asked.
Mara nodded and traced a line to the south. “Longer. Wider turn, though. We can pass the maintenance buildings and come in behind the station.”
“What's the downside?”
“Two extra kilometers, poor visibility at the drainage culvert, and Nico will complain about it.”
“I'm standing right here,” Nico said.
“Then I can strike the last one.”
Andrew studied the alternative route. Three weeks ago he might have made the decision before Mara had finished her explanation. Now he made himself ask the next question.
“Where would you bring a disabled machine around?”

Mara pointed out a hard-surfaced lot just beyond the culvert. She had already drawn the towing path in pencil. It would take longer, but none of their machines would have to back into the ditch to turn.
“That's the route,” Andrew said. “Mark the recovery point. We'll tell the others during checks.”
Mara looked pleasantly surprised for an instant, then disguised it by rolling up the map.
“You're getting easier to work with.”
“That's the nicest thing you've ever said to me.”
“Don't get used to it.”

Andrew watched her leave, the map tucked neatly under her arm. The morning schedule still had to be completed, the machines had to be inspected, and they had an afternoon test to run. Yet for the first time that day he felt a little less late.
At nine, the hangar doors were open enough to admit a gray stripe of daylight.

Inside, their XR-17s filled the maintenance bays like a line of resting animals. Each stood low on six articulated legs. Heavy armor covered the compact hulls, but joints and hydraulic lines remained visible wherever the plating needed to move. Their main cannons sat on rotating turrets above the angular cockpits, with matched upright missile pods on either side. Beneath each cockpit's armored brow, a smaller rotary cannon faced forward. The circular reactors projected from the rear of the machines, surrounded by cooling housings and service rails.

They were built to fight, not to be elegant. Up close, Andrew could see every repair their crews had made: replacement bolts in mismatched finishes, paint of slightly different shades, welds that no factory inspector would have accepted. Germany had produced the machines quickly enough to hold its ground when other defenses failed. Keeping these particular eight running was now up to the people living beside them.
Juno Kade was halfway underneath the left front leg of his machine.

Andrew recognized him by his bright golden-blond hair, which stuck out in directions no helmet could have caused. His orange goggles had been pushed up onto his forehead, and his headphones hung from the raised yellow collar of his dark jacket. A smear of black grease traveled from his wrist almost to his elbow.
“Morning,” Andrew called.
“Technically,” Juno replied from beneath the machine.
“What are we technically doing?”
“Removing a bearing.”
“Are we succeeding?”
“One of us is.”
Nico, kneeling beside a tray of parts, lifted a gloved hand. “That's me.”
Juno slid out on a low trolley and sat up. His bright blue eyes went from Andrew to the parts tray and back again.
“The left-front bearing's binding under load,” he said. “I felt it on the return yesterday. There's a replacement in stores, but the retaining collar doesn't want to come off.”

Andrew crouched to inspect the raised leg. A steel stand held its weight while the pistons were locked out. The bearing housing was partly disassembled, and the assembly had been marked so its alignment could be restored.
“You logged it?” Andrew asked.
“Yesterday.”
“And the new bearing?”
“Still wrapped. I was going to finish this before lunch, run a walking cycle, then check it again once everything cools.”
Andrew nodded. “Good. If it catches again, we ground the machine.”
Juno's mouth twisted. “You know what they sent us last time we asked for bearings?”
“A very polite refusal.”
“A request to explain why we couldn't reuse the old ones.”
Nico looked up. “We could send them the old one with a note saying it tried to eat the rest of the leg.”
“Don't,” Andrew said.
Juno considered it. “What if the note is formal?”
“Especially don't.”

On the next bay, a soft click sounded from a portable diagnostic screen. Sera Bell sat cross-legged on a crate with the cable looped around one knee. Her long curls were pinned into a loose bun, and she wore a large sweater over her work clothes. She was studying the recorded loads from Juno's last run.
“It's not just the bearing,” she said without looking up.
Juno turned. “You told me the bearing.”
“I told you the bearing was bad. There's also a loose vibration pickup on the left side. Your graph keeps saying the whole leg has fallen off, which would be more convincing if it actually had.”
Andrew glanced at the machine. “It hasn't, has it?”
Sera finally looked up.
“Not yet,” she said.
Juno groaned. “I knew you were going to say that.”

Sera unplugged the reader and held out the screen. She had highlighted the real bearing temperature and the false sensor spikes in different colors. Andrew saw the distinction immediately once she showed it to him.
“I can replace the pickup while he works on the collar,” Sera said.
“Do it,” Andrew answered. “And put both results on the inspection sheet. I want Mara to see them before we clear tomorrow's route.”
“You keep asking us to write down everything we fix,” Juno said.
“That's because you keep fixing things I didn't know were broken.”
“That's just good initiative.”
“It's excellent initiative,” Andrew said. “When it comes with paperwork.”
Juno sighed dramatically and rolled back under the leg.

Andrew stayed long enough to help Nico move the parts tray out of a puddle left by the leaking roof. He could have taken over. He knew how to hold the collar steady and how to thread the extractor, and the small voice that told him he'd sleep better if he did everything himself was already making its case.
Instead he left Juno to the work Juno knew best.
At the doors, he found Mara waiting with the revised map.
“Are we good?” she asked.
“Juno will tell us after the cold test. Sera's checking the sensor too.”
Mara studied his face. “And you didn't order them to let you help?”
“I moved a tray.”
“Miracles do happen.”
Andrew took the map from her. “Write that in the morning report.”
By midday, the rain had thinned to a mist.

Andrew spent the next hour at the north watch post, which was a generous name for a reinforced platform above the outer fence. The view was mostly fields, a narrow road, and the remains of an industrial building whose roof had collapsed long before their unit arrived. Farther out, the earth had been raised into defensive banks with concrete emplacements at intervals.

Yelena Sokolova was already there, leaning against the rail with a cup of tea. Her long braid was tucked inside her jacket against the wind. A battered paperback rested facedown on the ammunition locker beside her.
She glanced at Andrew. “You're early.”
“I'm on time.”
“Then the clock's wrong.”
“I'm deeply reassured by your confidence in me.”
“Someone has to keep your expectations reasonable.”

Andrew took the binoculars from their case. The road below was empty except for a flatbed truck heading west. Its load was hidden beneath a canvas cover, and the driver slowed as he passed the outpost to wave toward the tower.
Andrew raised a hand. The truck continued toward the interior settlements.

For a moment Andrew listened to its engine grow fainter. It wasn't much, but traffic still moved on some roads. People still carried materials, repaired their homes, quarreled over prices, and made deliveries that didn't involve weapons. On the base, it was easy to spend an entire day talking about machines and the next defensive line.
“Any movement?” he asked.
“Two patrol vehicles at the western junction,” Yelena said. “Three birds that nearly caused a diplomatic incident with the motion sensor. One truck with a suspiciously enthusiastic driver.”
“Sounds serious.”
“He waved twice.”
“Definitely suspicious.”
Yelena picked up her book, holding a finger between its pages to keep her place. Andrew noticed the cover: two people in very clean clothes standing in front of a lake.
“Good?” he asked.
“Terrible,” she answered.
“Then why are you on page two hundred?”
“To see if it gets worse.”
Andrew looked at the title. “It has a sequel.”
“Don't tell me things like that.”
He gave her the binoculars and opened the watch log. Yelena had recorded the vehicles, the weather, and a brief description of an animal near the fence.
“Small, four-legged, judgmental,” Andrew read.
“A cat,” Yelena said.
“Why didn't you write cat?”
“I wasn't sure it was ours.”
“Are cats normally assigned to us?”
“They should be. At least a cat would catch something around the ration store.”

They traded reports for a while. Yelena pointed out the swollen drainage channel that ran alongside the eastern road. Andrew could see why Mara had insisted on changing the patrol route. Brown water had spilled into the low ground, and the bridge approach was scarcely distinguishable from the field.
He used the tower radio to call Mara.
“You were right about the crossing,” he said when she answered.
There was a pause. “Say that again.”
“I said the eastern approach is underwater.”
“Not that part.”
Yelena reached over and pressed the transmit button. “Mara, he said you were right.”
“Thank you, Yelena,” Mara replied. “I'll note the time.”
Andrew took his hand off the radio.
“I work with children,” he said.
“You are younger than my favorite pair of boots,” Yelena answered.
“You're eighteen.”
“The boots are very old.”

On the way down, Andrew passed the outpost's little garden. Darius had built two raised beds against the kitchen wall using discarded transport crates. The plants were protected from the wind with clear plastic panels, and most were growing much more stubbornly than their surroundings suggested they should.
Darius was outside, holding a watering can in one hand and examining a row of herbs.
“Is there anything alive in there?” Andrew asked.
“Of course.”
“Anything edible?”
“That's a much more complicated question.”
Andrew looked at the tiny leaves. “How long until dinner?”
“Depends. What are you willing to eat?”
“Not the experimental porridge.”
Darius gave him an injured look. “It was one mistake.”
“And an ambitious one.”
Darius set down the can and brushed soil from his hands. “Dinner's going to be stew. I found beans, potatoes, and enough onions to pretend we planned ahead.”
“Excellent. What do you need?”
“For you to keep Nico away from the ingredients.”
“Unrealistic. Next request?”
“A clean pot.”
Andrew regarded him. “Surely that's the easy part.”
Darius turned toward the kitchen. “You'd think so.”
The afternoon test began just after two.

Juno brought his XR-17 out of the hangar at walking speed, moving across the concrete yard with the careful, uneven rhythm of a machine relearning how to use its legs. Each foot lifted, shifted, and settled with a dull mechanical thud. Heat shimmered behind the reactor housing. The cannon turret remained locked forward, and the missile bays were secured for maintenance.

Andrew stood beside Mara at a painted line a safe distance from the test area. Sera held a diagnostic tablet, its cable now connected to a short-range receiver. Nico wore hearing protection and carried the inspection clipboard as though he'd been promoted for the occasion.
Juno's voice came over their handheld radio.
“Left front leg responding. Load transfer normal. Ready for the turn.”
Mara checked the marked turning area. “Take the slow arc first. No clever tricks.”
“I'm wounded you even think that needs saying.”
“Nico suggested you climb the fuel shed to test clearance,” Mara replied.
From behind the clipboard, Nico said, “That was a theoretical suggestion.”
“It was a terrible theory,” Andrew said.
The XR-17 turned.

Its six feet worked in sequence, front and rear legs adjusting while the center pair carried the load. Andrew watched the left-front joint, where the old bearing had fought every step the day before. This time the foot came around smoothly.
“Temperature?” he asked Sera.
“Steady. More importantly, it's the actual temperature, not the sensor inventing a disaster.”
The machine completed the turn and came to a halt.
“Again,” Mara said over the radio. “Other direction.”
Juno obeyed. The second turn was slower but clean. They checked the data, then made him repeat the cycle with a slightly heavier load before agreeing to let him return to the bay.

When Juno climbed down, sweat had flattened his golden hair against his forehead. He came toward them grinning, with the satisfaction of someone who'd been proved right and intended to be gracious about it.
“She's perfect,” he said.
“She passed a walking test,” Mara corrected.
“Her walking is perfect.”
“Write that on the sheet,” Andrew told him. “Then do the cold check tonight.”
Juno's grin faltered. “You really enjoy paperwork.”
“I enjoy not having to explain why a leg came off.”
“It wouldn't have come off.”
Sera turned the tablet toward him. “That's what I said this morning. Nobody appreciated it.”
Nico ticked the last box on the inspection sheet. His handwriting crowded the margin, but every required test was there.
Andrew checked the page and handed it back. “Good work, all three of you.”
Nico brightened immediately. Juno tried not to look pleased and failed.
Akari appeared from behind the maintenance barrier, camera already in her hands.
“Wonderful,” she said. “The rain stopped. Everybody stay where you are.”
Mara looked at her boots. “We're covered in mud.”
“Authenticity.”
“I'm holding a diagnostic cable,” Sera said.
“Character.”
Andrew pointed toward the hangar. “You said four o'clock.”
“I'm doing practice shots.”
“You have been doing practice shots since breakfast.”
“Then imagine how good the real one will be.”
A drop of water landed on the camera's strap. Another hit Andrew's sleeve. Akari lifted her head as the fine mist became proper rain again.
She closed her eyes.
Nico looked toward the sky. “Maybe four o'clock.”
Akari lowered the camera carefully inside her jacket. “Nobody make plans after four.”
Andrew began to protest, remembered he'd already lost this argument, and let her have it.
At four seventeen, Akari declared that the weather was officially cooperating.

Andrew was not convinced. Water still dripped from the roof, and the sky over the depot looked capable of changing its mind at any moment. But the rain had stopped, and Akari stood in the courtyard with a tripod borrowed from the observation post and an expression that discouraged disagreement.
“Why are we doing this?” Mara asked.
“Because one day you'll thank me,” Akari said.
“Can I thank you from indoors?”
“Not while I'm taking the picture.”

Andrew had rounded up most of the others, though calling it rounding up made the task sound easier than it was. Yelena had to finish an entry in the watch log. Nico refused to appear until he found the jacket he considered his good one. Sera had been persuaded to put down her book after Akari threatened to photograph her reading it in the doorway.
Juno was the last to arrive. He came out of the hangar pulling his goggles from his hair, looking over his shoulder at the unfinished cleanup on his workbench.
“Two minutes,” he said. “I really should get that bearing sorted.”
“You replaced it already,” Andrew said.
“The old one. I want to see whether any of the race is worth recovering.”
“Tomorrow,” Akari announced.
“It's already tomorrow's work.”
“Then it's early.”

She positioned the eight of them in front of the center XR-17. Its body sat low between six angled legs, leaving just enough room beneath the hull for a row of people to look small and rather pleased about it. Juno asked if he could rotate the turret toward the camera; Mara vetoed the idea before he finished speaking.
“We're not moving a weapon for a photograph,” Mara said.
“It would look better,” Juno replied.
“We'll look alive,” Andrew told him. “That's better.”
Sera crouched to check the tripod's angle while Akari adjusted the lens. A strip of yellow tape marked the place where the front row needed to stand.
“You're all too far apart,” Akari said. “Move in.”
Nico shuffled closer to Darius, who was still wearing a dusting of flour on his sleeve.
“Closer.”
Nico pressed his shoulder against Darius's arm.
“Not inside him,” Akari said.
“Be specific,” Nico replied.
Yelena stood at the edge of the group with her arms crossed. Akari moved her beside Mara, who pointed out that her jacket was covered in mud.
“Everyone's jacket is covered in mud,” Akari said. “We're not taking a graduation portrait.”
“Some of us have standards,” Mara replied.
“You came here in boots that squeak.”
“They're waterproof.”
“They're making frog noises.”
Andrew could feel the argument gathering momentum. He stepped between them and spread his hands.
“New rule,” he said. “Nobody is allowed to criticize anyone's outfit until after the photograph.”
Sera looked at him. “Are you exempt?”
“Absolutely not.”
“Your collar's folded under,” she said.
Andrew fixed it. “Thank you. Last warning.”

Akari set the timer, then hurried toward the group. She had ten seconds. At six, she realized she'd left the camera strap hanging over the lens and doubled back. At four, she fixed it. At two, she sprinted forward.

Nico attempted to make room, stepped backward onto Mara's boot, and nearly toppled into Juno. Juno grabbed Nico's elbow. Mara grabbed Juno's collar. Andrew laughed at the sight of three people trying not to fall over.
The camera clicked.
Akari stood still for a beat, catching her breath.
“I hate all of you,” she announced.
“No, you don't,” Darius said.
She inspected the screen. Then her expression changed.
“Oh,” Akari said quietly. “Actually…”

The others crowded around her. The photograph showed all eight of them beneath the machine, their clothes untidy, several faces turned away from the camera. Nico's eyes were wide with alarm. Mara still had a fistful of Juno's jacket. Andrew was laughing, one hand stretched toward them, while Akari was just settling into the group.
It was an awful official portrait.
It was, Andrew thought, exactly how they looked.
“Delete it,” Mara said.
“Never,” Akari replied.
Darius leaned closer. “Can you print one for the kitchen?”
Akari looked up, delighted. “I can print eight.”
“Maybe one first,” Sera said. “We only have so much paper.”
Akari turned the camera toward Andrew. “Well?”
He looked at the faces again.
“Keep it,” he said.
Akari grinned. “Obviously.”
By five, the group had dispersed into the buildings and the courtyard was wet again.

Andrew was at his desk, trying to finish the patrol checklist, when Darius called his name from the kitchen. The difference between that call and the one from breakfast made Andrew stop writing immediately.
“Andrew. Come here.”
He found Darius standing beside the table with a large steel pot between his hands.
The pot was supposed to hold the stew they'd all been discussing since lunchtime.
Instead, an old bearing lay in the bottom of it, half submerged in cloudy brown liquid.
Black smears marked the rim. A folded shop rag sat beside it.
Juno stood against the counter. His shoulders were drawn in, and for once his mouth didn't seem to know what to do. Nico stood at his side, holding the lid.
Andrew looked into the pot, then at Juno.
“Explain.”
Juno rubbed the back of his neck. “The cleaning tray was being used, and I needed something wide enough to soak the old bearing.”
“That's our dinner pot,” Andrew said.
“I was going to wash it.”
Darius let out a sound that wasn't quite a laugh.
“With what?” he asked. “The dishes? You put machine grease and cleaning solvent in something we use for food.”
Juno glanced at the sink. “I didn't think—”
“No,” Darius said. “You didn't.”

The room went quiet. Darius rarely raised his voice; he didn't have to. His hands were flat against the table, and Andrew saw the row of prepared ingredients waiting untouched beside the stove. Darius had peeled the potatoes, chopped the cabbage, and carefully saved every onion he could find.
Nico set down the lid.
“I brought the pot,” he admitted. “Juno said he needed a container, and I knew where one was.”
“You knew where mine was,” Darius said.
Nico looked at the floor. “Yes.”
Juno straightened. “It was my idea. I should have asked. I'm sorry.”
Darius looked at him for a long moment.
“You could have ruined more than dinner,” he said.
“I know.”
“Do you?”
Juno met his eyes. “Yes. I do.”

Andrew opened his mouth with a suggestion about cleaning the pot, then stopped. Darius was right. It wasn't fit for food now, no matter how thoroughly somebody scrubbed it, and pretending otherwise wouldn't make the apology easier.

“It's out of the kitchen,” Andrew said. “Juno, take it to the workshop. We'll mark it for non-food use. You and Nico find Darius a replacement from stores, or work out a safe alternative with him until one arrives.”
Nico nodded quickly. Juno lifted the pot.
“Not above the vegetables,” Darius said.
“Right.”
Juno carried it around the other side of the table and out into the corridor. Nico followed him with the lid. Neither of them made a joke.
Andrew turned back to Darius.
“Can we help save dinner?” he asked.
Darius stared at the bowls. “I wanted to make a stew.”
“I know.”
“Real stew. Not ration paste with something green dropped in.”
Andrew waited.
Darius picked up a frying pan, tested its weight, and looked at the second one on the rack.
“We can fry the potatoes,” he said at last. “Put the cabbage and onions in with them. Beans in the small saucepan.”
“That sounds good.”
“It wasn't the plan.”
Andrew looked at the potatoes. “The plan changed. Happens to the best commanders.”
Darius gave him a tired look, then, despite himself, smiled.
“Get your sleeves rolled up,” he said.
Andrew did.
“What's my assignment?”
“Cabbage. Tear it into pieces. I'll tell you if they're wrong.”
It was a system Andrew understood.
Preparing dinner turned out to be louder than the repair test.
Nico returned from the workshop with clean hands, an apologetic expression, and a stack of bowls he had apparently collected in an effort to prove his usefulness.
Darius handed him a knife.
Nico stared at it. “Are you sure?”
“Potatoes,” Darius said. “Thin slices. Not a test of strength.”
Nico set the bowls aside and got to work.
Juno came back a few minutes later, wearing fresh sleeves and carrying the inventory book. He kept a careful distance from the stove.

“Stores doesn't have another pot that size,” he told Darius. “There's a smaller one in the vehicle workshop, but I haven't checked whether it's ever been used for anything else, so I'm not bringing it in.”
“Good,” Darius said.
“I wrote a request for a new one. And I can try the civilian kitchen depot next time we're cleared to go there.”
Darius turned a potato slice in the pan. “That's something.”
Juno hesitated. “Anything else I can do?”
Darius looked around the crowded kitchen. “Wash those bowls. In the sink. With the dish soap.”
“Understood.”
Andrew tore another handful of cabbage into pieces. He kept having to remind himself not to turn the job into strips of paper on a map. Cabbage was much less willing to follow instructions.
On the other side of the table, Nico held up a potato slice thick enough to balance on its edge.
Darius inspected it. “Smaller.”
“You said slices.”
“You've made a wheel.”
Andrew laughed. Nico pointed the knife at him.
“Away from people,” Darius said immediately.
Nico lowered it. “He's not helping.”
Darius gave Andrew another cabbage.
“He is now.”

The kitchen filled with the smell of onion, browned potato, and pepper. A little warmth leaked into the corridor. Whenever someone opened the door, somebody else appeared to ask when dinner would be ready.
Akari arrived to steal a test piece from the pan. Darius tapped her knuckles with the handle of the wooden spoon, not quite fast enough.
“Hot,” she said, chewing too quickly.
“Yes,” Darius replied.
Her eyes watered. Andrew handed her a cup of water without looking up from the cabbage.
Sera entered after Akari, carrying the projector remote in one hand and a folded piece of cardboard in the other. She took in the state of the kitchen and wisely stayed by the doorway.
“The projector works,” Sera announced.
“Did you fix the mount?” Juno asked.
“I fixed what was wrong with the picture.”
“That's not the same thing.”
“It's the part you can see.”
She held up the folded cardboard as evidence.
Juno opened his mouth. Andrew pointed a cabbage leaf toward him.
“You have enough technical arguments for one day.”
Juno closed his mouth, then went back to washing.

Mara stopped by with the completed route sheet. Andrew dried his hands before he touched it. The alternate path was marked clearly, along with two places to turn a damaged machine and the communication point where they would check in.
“Looks good,” he told her.
“You haven't read the whole thing.”
“I know the route. I read the changes.”
Mara checked the page herself. “And Juno's inspection?”
“Cold test still pending. It's on the list.”
She nodded, satisfied enough to fold the paper.
“Put it on my desk?” Andrew asked.
“You mean the desk you'll be sitting at after everyone else goes to bed?”
Andrew gave her a weary smile. “That desk.”
Mara didn't smile back right away.
“Don't make a hobby of it,” she said.
By the time dinner was ready, the common room had become almost comfortable.

The furniture was old and easy to clean, but the squad had done its best to make it less institutional. Cushions occupied chairs that were never supposed to have them. A bookshelf made from packing crates held novels, manuals, a deck of incomplete playing cards, and a small collection of objects nobody could explain. The old projector faced a bare patch of wall. A handwritten duty schedule hung beside a noticeboard crowded with reminders.

Andrew counted the places at the table as he brought in the last cups. Eight plates. Eight sets of cutlery. He couldn't remember when he'd started checking automatically, only that he always felt better once everyone had found a seat.
Darius entered carrying two pans and a saucepan.
“It's not stew,” he announced.
“Tragic,” Yelena said.
“It's also not porridge,” Nico added.
Darius set the pans down. “Keep going and you'll both be eating it outside.”
Everyone helped themselves. The potatoes had crisp brown edges and soft centers, and the onions had turned sweet in the pan. Darius watched the others for a moment before taking his own first bite.
Andrew made a point of tasting his portion.
Darius looked at him. “Well?”
“I'm still deciding.”
“You've eaten half of it.”
“It's a rigorous process.”
Darius rolled his eyes but finally relaxed into his chair.
Mara raised a particularly thick potato slice. “Nico, I think this one's yours.”
“How can you tell?” Nico asked.
“It has a structural foundation.”
Nico took a defensive bite of his dinner. “You all said I had to help.”
“We're grateful,” Andrew told him. “The roads could use more bricks.”
A short burst of laughter went around the table. Nico tried to look offended and couldn't sustain it.
Yelena produced the cards she'd brought from the watch post. “After dinner. Darius, I want a rematch.”
“You owe me two biscuits,” Darius said.
“An accounting disagreement.”
“You ate them.”
“Which is why I can't return them.”
“You could win replacements,” Andrew suggested.
Darius leaned forward. “I could win four.”
Yelena placed the deck on the table with a flourish. “You're very confident for someone who lost to me yesterday.”
“You changed the rules,” Darius said.
“You read the rules. You just didn't like the result.”
While they argued, Sera looked through the stack of films and old recordings beside the projector. Akari leaned over her shoulder, examining titles.
“Something funny,” Akari said.
“Define funny,” Sera answered.
“Something where the people don't spend the entire film making terrible decisions.”
Sera tapped one of the cases. “That excludes most comedies.”
“Then terrible decisions with a happy ending.”
Nico turned from his dinner. “Put on the one with the car chase.”
“We watched that last week,” Mara said.
“And it was good last week.”
“Nico,” Sera replied, “you spent the entire ending explaining how you could have driven better.”
“I could have.”
“You don't have a driver's license,” Andrew said.
“Not anymore.”
“Not ever,” Mara corrected.
Nico pointed a fork at her. “Small distinction.”
Juno set down his plate. “I could build a driving simulator for the projector.”
“No,” seven voices said at once.
For a moment Juno looked betrayed. Then he began laughing so hard that he had to lean against the back of his chair.

Andrew watched the others pick up the argument around him, as familiar as the warm smell of dinner and the uneven buzz of the projector's cooling fan. They argued about a film they'd all seen, over cards nobody was likely to win fairly, with the easy confidence of people who expected to see one another at breakfast.
He didn't need to settle any of it.
Darius caught his eye across the table. The cook had been listening to the argument with a small smile. He lifted his cup in Andrew's direction.
Andrew lifted his own.
For tonight, that was enough.
Yelena won the first card game.

Darius accused her of hiding a card. Yelena invited him to count the deck. He did, discovered it was complete, and demanded another round on the grounds that knowing the deck was complete should surely improve his chances.
It did not.

Andrew sat on the arm of the couch and watched the second game fall apart while Akari took a photograph of Darius's expression. Nico leaned over Mara's shoulder to give advice nobody had asked for. Mara threatened to charge him for every suggestion.
At the projector, Sera folded her piece of cardboard twice and slid it under one of the rear feet. The picture on the wall straightened.
“Fixed,” she said.
Juno, sitting on the floor with his repaired headphones around his neck, looked over. “You can't call that a repair.”
“Why not?”
“The mount needs replacing.”
“The film needs ninety minutes,” Sera answered. “I expect the cardboard can manage that.”
Akari applauded. Juno pretended to be insulted and then offered to find a better piece of cardboard.

By the time they settled on a film, somebody had taken the cushions from two chairs to build a more comfortable place on the floor. Nico complained that his preferred film hadn't won, despite having changed his vote twice. Darius brought out the last of the bread and warned everyone that there would be no second dinner.

Andrew checked the wall clock. He had one route to confirm, a note to add to Juno's inspection report, and a short briefing to prepare for morning. He could have finished most of it before dinner. He could also finish it in ten minutes now.
He stayed for the first part of the film.

The hero, a man in an immaculate suit, was attempting to get through a kitchen window without being noticed. Nico insisted that the obvious solution was to break the glass. Sera pointed out that the entire point of the scene was not being noticed. Nico maintained that the glass should simply have been quieter.
Andrew laughed until his eyes watered.
Eventually he slipped away while the room was busy arguing about whether the hero had deserved to get caught.

His office was cool after the packed common room. He switched on the desk lamp, unfolded Mara's route sheet, and checked the approach one final time. The service road gave the patrol a little more room and a safer retreat. Juno's cold test had been scheduled and signed for; his machine would remain grounded if the inspection failed. Andrew made that note in the morning orders.
The room next door burst into laughter. Someone complained about the volume. Someone else made it louder.
Andrew looked down at the map. There was still more he could do. Another route to compare. Another possible failure to imagine. He had been very good at imagining failures since taking command.
He reached for his coffee, remembered the mug was empty, and set it aside.
A photograph was pinned to the wall beside his desk lamp.

Twelve young soldiers stood between two XR-17s, pressed together because Akari had insisted that everyone fit. The picture had been taken on a dry day. Their uniforms were less worn, and most of them were grinning at something outside the frame.

Matthias Adler stood at the back, taller than several of the others, with two fingers hooked into Andrew's collar. Andrew remembered trying to pull free just as Akari called for them to look at the camera. Matthias had laughed and refused to let go.
Andrew could no longer remember what the joke had been.
He straightened the corner of the photograph where it had curled from the wall and went back to the route sheet. He didn't need to study the picture to remember the faces.
A knock sounded at the door.
Darius stood in the corridor holding a small plate and a jar.
“Are you hiding?” he asked.
“Working.”
“I can see that. Are you hiding while you work?”
Andrew smiled. “Depends who you're asking.”

Darius came in and set the plate on the one corner of the desk not covered by paper. A bread roll lay on it, sliced and toasted. He unscrewed the little jar and spread a careful layer of jam all the way to the edges.
Andrew stared at the label.
“Strawberry? Where did you get that?”
“I have arrangements,” Darius said.
“With who?”
“People who appreciate bread.”
Andrew took a bite. The toast crackled, and for a few seconds the sweet taste occupied his attention completely.
“That's good,” he said.
“It's jam on bread.”
“Don't undersell your work.”
Darius leaned against the filing cabinet. He looked tired now, his apron gone and his sleeves rolled to the elbows.
“I wasn't happy about the pot,” he said.
“You had every right.”
“I know. I just don't want Juno thinking I'm going to hold it against him forever.”
“He doesn't. I think he wants to replace your entire kitchen.”
“Tell him to start with a pot.”
“I'll put it in writing.”
Darius smiled, then looked at the route sheet.
“You finished?”
“Almost.”
“How much is almost?”
Andrew glanced at the clock. “Ten minutes.”
“You told me ten minutes after breakfast.”
“That was a different ten minutes.”
“Of course.”
For a while Darius stayed where he was, not pressing. A cheer went up from the common room, followed by Nico loudly demanding that somebody replay the last scene.
Andrew looked at the map again. The route was marked. Mara had checked it. The inspection had a clear condition for approval. The morning briefing could be read without another hour of polishing.
He placed his pencil across the paper.
“If Nico picked the film after all, I'm blaming you.”
Darius pushed away from the cabinet. “Fair.”
Andrew picked up the plate and followed him back down the corridor.
A space had appeared on the couch beside Akari. She lifted her feet just long enough for him to sit and then laid them across his knees again.
“I charge for this,” Andrew told her.
“Put it on my account.”

On the wall, the man in the immaculate suit was now hanging from the kitchen window by his belt. Sera announced that they had reached the part of the story where everyone's advice would be useless. Nico protested that he had plenty of useful advice, and Mara told him that was precisely the problem.
Andrew settled back, the plate balanced on one hand.
Akari reached for his toast.
He caught her wrist without looking away from the film.
“Ask Darius.”
“I did,” she said. “He said you'd share.”
Across the room Darius was explaining the rules of a third card game to Yelena, who had already begun planning how to win it. He caught Andrew's expression and gave him a small, unrepentant shrug.
Andrew broke the toast in half.
Akari accepted her share, and the two of them watched the rest of the film with their friends.
